Age decay (`bb12d3`) is closed as delivered. It is installed but **unfed**: most accepted references carry no publication date, so the signal is a near-constant and changes nothing.

## Measured 2026-07-27 (read-only, on `fix/recency-prefer-publication-date`)

| Corpus | Accepted | with `sourcePublishedAt` or `sourceUpdatedAt` |
|---|---:|---:|
| ai-ml-research | 1376 | **316 (23.0%)** |
| threat-intelligence | 13 | **1 (7.7%)** |

Corroborating evidence: `retrieval_post_hybrid_a61c12` and `retrieval_post_recency_bb12d3` are identical to four decimals — `mrr_sum` included. Landing age decay moved literally nothing.

Before `TI-f1cc13`, recency read `max()` across six date keys including `retrievedAt`/`importedAt`, so ~all documents scored ~1.0 (maximally fresh). After the fix, the 77% / 92% without publication dates score a neutral 0.5. **The fix is correct** — 0.5 is honest where 1.0 was a lie — but honest-and-inert is still inert. Recency consumes 7% of the ranking weight budget and conveys nothing for most of the corpus.

## Related, and closed too early

Bug `71ce66` — "Accession leaves `sourcePublishedAt`/`retrievedAt` null so age-decay `sourcePublishedAtDay` cannot land" — is **closed**. The coverage numbers above say the problem is still here. Either that fix only covered newly accessioned references and never backfilled the existing 1060, or it is not holding. Establish which before writing new code; do not assume.

## Work

1. **Extract publication dates at ingestion.** PDFs: GROBID/Biblicus already parse metadata — check whether a date is being extracted and dropped on the floor rather than absent. HTML: `<meta>` (`article:published_time`, `citation_publication_date`, `dcterms.date`), JSON-LD `datePublished`, and `<time datetime>`. Most threat-intel vendor posts and advisories carry at least one.
2. **Backfill existing accepted references** from already-archived source bytes and `extracted_text`. No re-fetch — per the initiative, everything needed is already stored.
3. **Re-run the golden set** and report whether recency now moves anything. If coverage rises substantially and rankings still do not change, that is a real finding: say so, and the 7% weight should be reconsidered rather than defended.

## Constraints

- **Never** let `retrievedAt` or `importedAt` back into the recency path. That was `TI-f1cc13`; a backfill that fills `sourcePublishedAt` *from* an ingestion timestamp reintroduces the same bug wearing a different field name. Absent is better than fabricated.
- Where no date can be found, leave it null. `recencyKnown=false` exists precisely for this.
- Report coverage before and after as counts, not just percentages.

issues.description:
The hybrid-lexical build surfaced 55 accepted references in `knowledge-corpus-ai-ml-research` with no `extracted_text` attachment — 4% of that corpus.

They were correctly skipped by the lexical builder, and the same extractability gate applies to vector passages. So these references are **accepted, evidence-eligible in principle, and unfindable by either retriever in practice.** A human decided they belonged in the corpus and the system cannot surface them.

## Why this matters more than it looks

This is not a lexical-index defect — the builder did the right thing and now records it in the manifest. It is a corpus-health gap that was invisible until an index build counted it.

The curation gate is the editorial guarantee: accepted means a person chose this source. A reference that passes that gate but can never be retrieved quietly breaks the guarantee, because the publication cannot cite what it cannot find. It also means every retrieval metric in this initiative was computed over a denominator 4% smaller than the accepted corpus, without anyone knowing.

## What to determine

1. **Why they lack extracted text.** Likely a mix: accession failures, unsupported media types, sources that were already dead by the time extraction ran, PDFs GROBID could not parse. Classify them — the counts will point at the fix.
2. **Whether they are recoverable.** For any with a live `sourceUri` or an archived `role="source"` attachment, re-running extraction may be enough. Those are cheap wins.
3. **Whether the number is growing.** A one-time historical residue is very different from an ongoing leak in the accession path. Check when these references were accepted.
4. **Whether accession should fail loudly.** If extraction fails, the reference currently proceeds to accepted with no retrievable text and nothing signals it. Recording an explicit state — or surfacing a "accepted but not retrievable" count in a routine report — would stop the next 55 accumulating silently.

## Related

- `kanbus-ea1686` covers 3 references blocked at canonical-source resolution — a different failure, same family.
- The end-to-end ingestion exercise (`TI-c46828`) will run accession on fresh sources and may reproduce the cause directly, which would be the fastest route to a diagnosis.

Not urgent. But worth doing before the corpus grows, since the same gap at ten times the volume is 550 references nobody can retrieve.
issues.title: 55 accepted references have no extracted text and cannot be retrieved

comments.text:
Golden-set defect found during the age-decay epic (kanbus-bb12d3): the `freshness` category does not test what its name implies.

Four of its five queries return the expected reference at rank 1, so there is no ordering for a recency signal to influence. The fifth (`q-fresh-4`) is `rank=-1` — not retrieved at all — so it is a recall failure a tie-breaker cannot reach.

A category meant to test stale-vs-fresh preference needs cases where **both** a stale and a fresh reference are retrievable and relevant, and only their relative order is in question. As built, the category cannot validate any ranking-order change.

This is the second acceptance criterion in this initiative set against an instrument that could not observe the change (the first: passage scoring measured against a golden set that scores reference rank). When this epic is picked up, the general fix is worth stating: **a golden query is only useful for validating a change if the change can, in principle, alter its result.** Categories should be designed against the mechanism they test, not named after the intuition.

issues.description:
A decision issue, not an implementation issue. Read it before picking up Phase 2.

## The numbers that prompt this

- `knowledge-corpus-threat-intelligence`: **13 accepted references.** Thirteen.
- `knowledge-corpus-ai-ml-research`: 1376 accepted references.
- The golden set (25 queries) evaluates **ai-ml-research only**. Every number this initiative has reported — baseline 0.653, post-hybrid 0.853, Hit@5 76% → 96% — is from the AI/ML corpus.
- The provenance note on the latest report says it plainly: *"Threat-intel exact-token retrieval (CVE / hash / ATT&CK) is still unmeasured."*

## What that means

This initiative's stated purpose was retrieval that handles **this domain's** exact identifiers — CVE IDs, file hashes, actor aliases, ATT&CK IDs. That capability was built, and it was validated against a corpus of AI/ML research papers, where the "identifier" queries are arXiv IDs and model names. **The capability built for CVE/hash/ATT&CK has never once been tested on CVE/hash/ATT&CK.**

Meanwhile the publication those identifiers serve has a thirteen-document corpus. No amount of ranking quality makes thirteen documents into a knowledge base.

The initiative already flags this as a live question: *"the binding constraint on publication quality may now be corpus size rather than retrieval quality — which is curation throughput, not ranking. Worth re-deciding rather than proceeding by momentum."* The coverage data now answers it. Proceeding into Phase 2 (entity extraction → resolution → contextual chunks) would be momentum.

Note that Phase 2's own sequencing note already concedes the point — entity resolution is *"deliberately follows corpus growth: resolution's value is proportional to alias fragmentation, which barely exists yet."* With 13 documents there is no alias fragmentation to resolve. The precondition Phase 2 was told to wait for has not happened.

## The decision to make

**Option A — pivot to corpus growth.** Treat curation throughput and ingestion as the initiative's remaining work. Assisted triage (`TI-c21d28` and follow-ons) is already built and nearly landed; the 43 references awaiting curation are the immediate test of it. Phase 2 waits for a corpus worth extracting entities from.

**Option B — continue Phase 2 on ai-ml-research**, accepting that it serves the P.apyr.us publication rather than Threat Intelligence, and that TI retrieval stays unmeasured.

**Option C — build a TI golden set first** (~15 queries against the 13 real references plus whatever curation admits), measure identifier retrieval where it was actually meant to work, then decide with data instead of inference.

C is cheap and unblocks a defensible choice between A and B. It is probably the first move regardless — but the decision is the operator's, and the point of this issue is to make it deliberately.

## Prerequisite

Do not build a TI golden set until `TI-b9f6da` is fixed. A new golden set measured against a broken lexical arm would bake the regression into the baseline and make it permanent.
issues.title: Decide: threat-intelligence corpus is 13 references and retrieval there is unmeasured

issues.description:
`PASSAGE_HEADING_BOOSTS` in `src/papyrus_knowledge_query/engine.py` now hardcodes two publications' document structures — academic paper sections (abstract, introduction, evaluation, results) and threat-intel report sections (executive summary, IOCs, attribution, detections). Both sets live in shared engine code that every Papyrus instance runs.

## Why this is wrong

`kanbus-5c7cde` existed because passage scoring was overfit to one corpus. We fixed it by adding a second corpus's overfit alongside the first. That is better than before — this instance genuinely ingests both — but it does not scale and it inverts the architecture: a legal, medical, or financial publication makes it three domains in a file none of them should have to care about.

Papyrus is a general CMS. One installation is one publication, and what counts as a high-value section is a property of *that publication's source material*, not of the retrieval engine. The engine should know that headings can be weighted; it should not know what "MITRE ATT&CK Mapping" is.

Note the identifier layer already gets this right: `_normalize_doi`, `_normalize_arxiv_id`, `_normalize_isbn`, `_normalize_pmid` are per-type normalizers composing into a general capability, with no publication assuming primacy. Heading profiles should follow that shape.

## Proposed direction

Move heading weights into per-corpus configuration. `corpora/papyrus-steering.yml` already declares corpora with `key`, `role`, and `localClassifiers`, so a `passageHeadings` block per corpus is a natural extension and keeps publication-specific knowledge in publication-specific config:

```yaml
corpora:
  - key: "threat-intelligence"
    passageHeadings:
      "executive summary": 8
      "iocs": 6
```

Design points worth settling during implementation, not now:

- **Fallback when a corpus declares nothing.** A small structural default (a first-section bias) is probably better than zero weighting, but it must not be either domain's vocabulary.
- **Multi-corpus instances.** This installation has one corpus declared but the AI/ML instance may have several; resolution should key off the reference's `corpusId`, which the passage path already has.
- **Keep the engine's default empty.** If `PASSAGE_HEADING_BOOSTS` survives as a constant it will drift back into a dumping ground. Better that the engine ships no domain vocabulary at all.

## Not urgent

The current state is functional and correct for this instance. This is architectural hygiene to do before a third publication exists, not a bug to fix now. Sequence it after the hybrid-lexical epic, since that work touches the same scoring path and will make the seams clearer.
issues.title: Move passage heading weights out of engine code into per-corpus config

Verified and accepted. Both halves of this are right, and the second one is worth more than the fix.

**Confirmed independently:**

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| scoped rebuild, eligible 1376 → 1 | **BLOCKED** |
| normal drift 1376 → 1370 | allowed |
| 1376 → 1 with `allow_shrink` | allowed |
| Papyrus-main artifact after your read-only run | still 1321 / 5658 / 1376 |

Suite: 469 passing against 462 on develop, and 12 failures against 13 — you added tests and fixed one pre-existing failure along the way.

**The merge fix is the correct fix.** A scoped sync should update the lineages it was asked about and leave the rest alone; remapping postings so survivors need no re-tokenisation is the right shape.

**The guard is the more valuable half, and I want to name why.** The fix stops this bug. The guard stops the *class* — any future change that publishes a catastrophically smaller index now fails loudly instead of silently degrading retrieval until someone notices results got worse. Refusing the promote rather than warning is the right call: a warning in a long sync log is a warning nobody reads.

Two details you got right that are easy to get wrong: the `≥10` floor means small and first-time indexes are not tripped by their own growth, and `allow_shrink` being unavailable to scoped syncs closes the obvious escape hatch — the operator who hits the guard during a `--reference-id` run cannot make it go away by adding `--force`, which is exactly when they would be most tempted.

This is the third instance of the same underlying failure mode in this initiative — silent partial work that looks like success. The `except: pass` that disabled archival, the eval measuring something other than the change, and now an index that publishes itself smaller. Each time the fix has been to make the failure loud at the point it happens. Worth keeping as a design instinct rather than a rule: **if a component can do less than asked without erroring, it will eventually do so unobserved.**

Merging.

## Before you change anything: the observation is right, the diagnosis is probably wrong

`Reference.metadata` being null is **by design**, not a bug. `model_attachments.py:327` does:

```python
elif record["modelName"] == "Reference" and "metadata" in expected:
    metadata = parse_jsonish(expected.pop("metadata"))
```

It **pops** the field off the record and writes it to a `ModelAttachment` with `role="metadata"`, because DynamoDB items have a size limit and large payloads are offloaded to S3. Every accepted reference in this corpus works that way. So "Reference.metadata stays null" is the system behaving correctly.

**The real question is whether `registration_note` reaches that attachment.** Check that first, because it decides which layer is broken:

- **If the note is in the `role="metadata"` attachment**: the write path is fine and the bug is in whatever read `Reference.metadata` directly and found nothing — likely the queue builder. Fix the reader. Do not touch the intake path.
- **If the note is absent from the attachment too**: the bug is upstream in `catalog.py`. `item_registration_note` is computed at `:286-289` and feeds `curation_note`, but confirm it actually lands in `normalized_metadata` (`:299`) rather than only being used for the curation note.

Concretely: pick one of the 18 new prospects, fetch its `ModelAttachment` rows, find `role="metadata"`, and read the content. That single check tells you which fix to make.

## Why this matters beyond the bug

The rationale is what makes a review queue reviewable. Without it a prospect is a URL and a title, and the operator has to reconstruct context the machine already had. It is also the input to `kanbus-ec5555` (grounding triage rationales) — the 30-item session found 0/30 rationales sufficient to decide from without opening the source, and missing provenance is part of why.

Together with `TI-1ad2f4`, this is why the ingestion exercise had to write an `operator-queue.json` sidecar: the schema currently cannot answer "what is in my review queue and why is each item here." That sidecar is a symptom. Fix these two and the queue derives from the data model.

### Next checks (still open)

Why the eval/process did not get lexical hits: bucket/env for `BM25LexicalProvider`, swallowed exception in warnings, or provider `None`. Do **not** rebuild the artifact until that is recorded.

### Related work in flight on TI-5ed2f2

Eval harness will set `PAPYRUS_REQUIRE_LEXICAL=1` and preflight lexical floors so this failure mode cannot produce a “valid” golden report. Engine raises under that flag; default runtime still falls back with a warning (now also when provider is missing).

The identifier category — the headline achievement of this initiative — scores **0/5 on `develop` today**. Fix this before trusting any other retrieval measurement.

## Evidence

| Report | commit | identifier | MRR |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| `retrieval_baseline.json` (pre-hybrid) | — | 0/5 | 0.6533 |
| `retrieval_post_hybrid_a61c12.json` | a61c12 | **5/5** | 0.8533 |
| `retrieval_post_recency_bb12d3.json` | bb12d3 | **5/5** | 0.8533 |
| `retrieval_post_pubdate_bfc2f3.json` | bfc2f33, 2026-07-27 | **0/5** | 0.6533 |

Reproduced on parent `beab60a` under the same environment, so it is **not** caused by the prefer-publication-date change. The four non-identifier categories are bit-identical throughout.

**The MRR is exactly the pre-hybrid baseline — 0.6533, to four decimals.** That is the tell. This is not a degraded lexical arm returning weaker hits; the system is scoring as though the lexical arm contributes *nothing at all*. Fusion is running with one arm.

## Leading hypothesis, in the order worth checking

1. **The lexical artifact was overwritten with a subset.** Closed bug `9b6971` — "`knowledge-vector-index --reference-id` rebuilds lexical index for that subset only" — describes exactly this failure. The bug is closed, but closing the code path does not repair an artifact already clobbered by it. Check `corpora/knowledge-index/lexical/v1/index.json.gz`: how many documents does it actually contain? Compare against 1376 accepted in `knowledge-corpus-ai-ml-research`.
   - Note `assert_lexical_promote_safe` (`LEXICAL_SHRINK_GUARD_RATIO = 0.5`, `MIN_EXISTING = 10`) only blocks a shrink *below half*. A subset rebuild of 60% passes the guard silently. And the guard cannot fire at all on a path that does not call it.
2. **The artifact is missing or unreadable from the eval environment** — wrong bucket, wrong prefix, credentials, region. If the loader swallows that and falls back to semantic-only, it would produce exactly this signature. **If a silent fallback exists, that is a second bug: it must fail loudly.**
3. **The long-standing corpus gap.** The initiative has carried an unexplained "99-reference gap between the lexical artifact (1321) and the live accepted corpus (1420)" since `a61c12` landed. It was never explained. Accepted is now 1376. Resolve this number properly rather than noting it again.

## Acceptance

- Identifier back to **5/5**, global MRR ≈ **0.8533**, on `develop`, in a report committed with the usual provenance block.
- State the lexical artifact's document count and the accepted-reference count **in the report note**, as two explicit numbers. This gap has been carried as a footnote for weeks; make it a measured field so drift is visible next time.
- If the cause was a silent fallback or a guard that could not fire, fix that too and add a test. An index that quietly serves nothing is the recurring failure mode of this whole initiative: silent partial work that looks like success.

## Do not

- Do not re-tune ranking weights to recover MRR. The retrieval logic is not what changed.
- Do not rebuild the lexical artifact until you have recorded what the current one contains. The broken state is the evidence.

comments.text:
## Correction — the gap is bigger than "nothing reads Assignments"

My original framing was imprecise. Inspecting `.papyrus-runs/ec5555-batch/human-queue.json` (43 items) shows three distinct layers, only two of which are persisted:

| Layer | Where it lives |
|---|---|
| The References | GraphQL — 1024 pending |
| "Needs review" | GraphQL — 46 open curation Assignments |
| **Lane, clusterId / clusterPrimary / clusterSiblingIds, evidence, mechanicalAction, autoArchiveRule, exploratory** | **only the plan file** |

So the records are in the API. The **triage judgment layer** is not — it is recomputed on every `triage-plan` run and written to a gitignored file that expires with its run directory.

That layer is what makes the queue reviewable. Without it an operator has 1024 pending References with no way to tell which are new, which are duplicates of each other, or why any of them is worth attention.

## The real design question

Not "read the Assignments" — that alone would produce an unranked, unexplained list. The question is whether lane, cluster membership, and evidence should **persist**, and where.

Consequences of the current recompute-every-run design:

- A half-worked review session cannot resume; the lanes are gone unless the plan file survives.
- A UI (`kanbus-4d5390`) must recompute the whole triage before rendering anything, over an unfiltered listing of four models.
- Two runs over the same corpus can legitimately disagree — thresholds are constants today, but the accepted/rejected history they read is not, so lane assignment drifts as curation proceeds. Nothing records which computation an operator was looking at when they decided.

Options worth weighing rather than assuming:

1. **Persist the triage result** — lane, cluster, evidence on the curation Assignment, written when `triage-plan` runs. Queue becomes queryable, sessions resumable, decisions attributable to a specific triage. Cost: another write path, and staleness when the corpus moves under it.
2. **Persist only cluster membership** (a genuinely corpus-level fact, arguably a `SemanticRelation`) and recompute lane/evidence per session as cheap derived output.
3. **Keep recompute, make the plan a first-class artifact** — durable location, addressable id, referenced from the Assignment. Least change; still leaves the queue invisible to anything but the CLI.

I lean 2: cluster membership is a fact about the corpus and belongs in the graph, while lane and evidence are judgments relative to a moment and a threshold set, which are better recomputed than staled. But this is a design call worth making deliberately, not by picking whichever is easiest to implement.

Whatever is chosen, the loop still needs closing: nothing transitions a curation Assignment when `review_reference_curation` records a decision, so the 46 `open` rows will drift from reality as soon as curation starts.

comments.text:
## Approved design — triage state moves into GraphQL

Papyrus is a multi-agent system in which the AppSync API is the coordination substrate. A run-scoped local file is invisible to other agents, to a second machine, to the Newsroom UI, and to the next run. My earlier "recompute per session" recommendation assumed a single-operator CLI and is **withdrawn**.

**Nothing needs a new top-level model.** This decomposes onto three patterns already in the codebase.

### (a) Run-level plan → a `Message`, copying `research_packet` exactly

Research already solves this problem. `apply_research_packet` (`assignments_workflow.py:865`) writes a `Message` with `messageKind="research_packet"`, payload auto-offloaded to a `ModelAttachment(role="metadata")` by `expand_private_payload_records`, linked to its Assignment by a `SemanticRelation` with predicate `produces`. `load_assignment_research_packet_entries` (`:1327`) reads it back through the `subjectStateKey` / `objectStateKey` GSIs with **no table scan**.

Copy that shape with `messageKind="curation_triage_plan"`. Use a deterministic content-addressed id the way `research_packet_hash` (`:1775`) does, so concurrent planners converge on the same row rather than conflicting — that is this codebase's concurrency style and a better fit here than locking.

The `produces` seed (`corpora/papyrus-semantic-relation-types.yml:344-354`) already permits `assignment → message`, so no relation-type change. `Message` is a `realtimeModel`, so the UI gets subscriptions free.

### (b) Per-item current state → new `Assignment` fields + one composite GSI

The `curation.reference-intake` Assignment is already 1:1 with a pending Reference and idempotently keyed on `[corpusId, referenceLineageId]` (`catalog.py:517-520`). Add `triageLane`, `triageClusterId`, `triageClusterPrimary`, `triageRationale`, `triageRunId`, `triageUpdatedAt`, `triageMechanicalRule`, `triageMechanicalAction`, `triageMechanicalReasonCode`.

Derive `triageQueueLaneKey = "<queueKey>#<status>#<lane>"` in `add_operational_index_fields` (`graphql_authoring.py:885`), exactly as `KnowledgeImportRun.corpusImportKindKey` is derived. Index it with sort keys `priority, createdAt`.

**Two things that already work and should be used rather than scanned around:** `queueStatusKey` + `listAssignmentsByQueueStatusAndPriority` already answers "open assignments in corpus X" with no schema change, and `listReferencesByCurationStatusKeyAndUpdatedAt` (`schema.ts:1306`) exists but is not registered in `INDEX_DEFINITIONS` — registering it removes the Reference scan outright.

### (c) Decisions → `AssignmentEvent` + metadata attachment

`reporting_packet_review.py:97-116` is the precedent and `AGENTS.md:194-201` blesses it: non-lifecycle decisions use `AssignmentEvent.eventType` with structured metadata in an event-owned `ModelAttachment`. Use `curation_triage_*` types. Zero schema change.

**Close the loop.** `review_reference_curation` (`reference_actions.py:170`) must transition the Assignment on decision. Nothing does today, so the 46 `open` rows drift from reality the moment curation starts.

### Housekeeping this forces

- `ASSIGNMENT_FIELDS` (`graphql_authoring.py:56-61`) must gain the new fields or reads silently return `None`.
- `catalog.py:536-537` writes `brief` and `instructions`, which do not exist in the deployed schema and are silently stripped. Delete them.
- **`amplify/data/schema.ts` is the deployed schema.** The large inline schema in `resource.ts` is dead — only its type is exported. Confirmed against `amplify_outputs.json`.

### Deploy caution — new for this initiative

This is the first change here that alters the deployed schema. Use `ampx` against the **sandbox only**. Do not run production deploys locally; per `AGENTS.md` Core Rules those go through the pipeline from `main`. Verify against sandbox, then hand the schema change over rather than deploying it yourself.

### Acceptance

The real test is not "the queue renders." It is: **read the queue from a second process with no access to `.papyrus-runs/` and get the same answer.** Also confirm the read is index-only rather than scanning, that running the planner twice produces one plan Message rather than two, and that accepting a reference moves its Assignment out of `open`.

comments.text:
## Sandbox deploy failed — drop the GSI. My design error.

```
A resolver can only be composed of 10 functions. (Service: AppSync, Status Code: 400)
Failed to create: [QuerylistAssignmentsByTriageQueueLaneAndPriorityResolver]
Failed to update:  [UpdateAssignmentResolver, DeleteAssignmentResolver]
```

Stack rolled back cleanly (`UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE`); the sandbox is back to its prior state and nothing is damaged.

**Cause.** `Assignment` already has **9 GSIs** (`newsroomFeedKey`, `queueStatusKey`, `assignmentTypeKey`, `status`, `assigneeKey`, `importRunId`, `sectionStatusKey`, `sectionKey`, `sectionQueueStatusKey`). Amplify generates one pipeline function per index on the create/update/delete resolvers to keep indexes consistent, and AppSync caps a pipeline resolver at 10 functions. The tenth index blows the ceiling — which is why *Update* and *Delete* failed alongside the new query resolver.

The exploration I commissioned reported "9 GSIs" plainly. I wrote "add one composite GSI" without connecting that number to the AppSync limit. That is on me, not on the implementation.

## The fix: no GSI, filter in memory

`queueStatusKey = "curation.reference-intake#<corpusId>#open"` with `listAssignmentsByQueueStatusAndPriority` **already** returns exactly the corpus's open curation queue in one indexed query. That partition is 46 items today and bounded by pending-review depth — hundreds at worst, because it drains as humans work it.

Filtering that result by `triageLane` in memory is free at this scale. The index was an optimisation for a scale we do not have, and adding it cost a deploy failure.

This is the principle I have been applying to every other epic and failed to apply to my own plan: **do not build machinery whose value scales with corpus size while the corpus is small.**

Concretely:
1. Remove `index("triageQueueLaneKey")...` from `amplify/data/schema.ts`.
2. Remove the `triageQueueLaneKey` field too — without the index it carries no meaning, and a derived key nothing reads is a maintenance trap. Drop its computation from `add_operational_index_fields`.
3. Keep `triageLane` as a plain attribute. In `list_open_curation_queue`, query `assignmentsByQueueStatusAndPriority` and filter on `triageLane` client-side. Keep the function signature — callers should not care.
4. Everything else in the design stands unchanged: the `curation_triage_plan` Message, the triage attributes on `Assignment`, the `AssignmentEvent` decisions, closing the loop on accept. Those are the parts that put the queue in the API; the index was never load-bearing for that.

**If lane-indexed queries are ever genuinely needed**, the options are to retire one of the three `section*` GSIs, or fold lane into `queueStatusKey` rather than adding a parallel key. Neither is worth doing now — record the constraint and move on.

## Two things worth capturing beyond this fix

**`ampx sandbox --once` exited 0 on a failed deployment.** The CloudFormation error was printed and the process still returned success. Anything that trusts the exit code — CI, a script, an agent checking `$?` — will read a rolled-back deploy as a green one. Worth a note wherever deploy guidance lives, and worth grepping output for `[ERROR]` rather than trusting the code.

**Assignment is now one index from its ceiling**, permanently. That is a real architectural constraint on a central model and nothing in the repo records it. Whoever next reaches for an Assignment GSI should find this written down rather than discovering it through a rollback. Worth a line in `AGENTS.md` alongside the other schema rules.

The review queue now exists in GraphQL, and nothing reads it. That is why an operator still gets handed a JSON file.

## Observed

After `TI-1ad2f4`, the write path works: **46 open curation Assignments**, one per prospect from the research batch, sitting in the API right now alongside their `Reference` rows and the `role=metadata` ModelAttachments carrying `registrationNote`.

The read path does not exist:

- `assisted_curation_triage.py` contains **zero** references to `Assignment`. It builds its queue by listing `Reference`, `ReferenceAttachment`, `Message`, `SemanticRelation`, and `Category`, computing lanes and rationales in memory, and writing them to a plan file.
- No command lists curation Assignments as a queue.
- The operator's queue therefore lives in `.papyrus-runs/<run>/human-queue.json` — a gitignored, machine-local artifact that expires with the run directory.

So the JSON is not standing in for the schema. It is standing in for a **reader**. We built the record and never built the thing that surfaces it.

## Why this matters

The consequences are ordinary but real:

- The queue is invisible to anything except the CLI session that produced it — no Newsroom UI, no second machine, no continuity across runs.
- Review state has nowhere durable to live. An Assignment can carry claimed/in-progress/completed; a plan file cannot, so a partially worked queue is lost.
- Every triage run recomputes lanes from an unfiltered listing of four models (`references_commands.py:142-149`). That is already the wrong shape at 1024 pending references and gets worse linearly.
- The Assignment rows exist and go stale: nothing ever closes them when a reference is accepted, so `open` will drift from reality immediately.

## What to build

1. **Read the queue from Assignments.** `triage-plan` should source its candidate set from open curation Assignments rather than from a full `Reference` listing, joining the reference, its `role=metadata` attachment for `registrationNote`, and its computed lane.
2. **Close the loop.** `review_reference_curation` should transition the corresponding Assignment when a decision lands. Without this the queue only grows.
3. **Add a plain queue command** — something an operator can run to see open curation assignments with rationale, without producing a plan file first. The plan file should be an artifact of a triage *session*, not the only way to see what needs review.
4. Keep the plan file for what it is good at: a reproducible snapshot of one triage run, with its lane assignments and thresholds recorded.

## Related

`kanbus-4d5390` (Newsroom UI for assisted curation triage) is the eventual surface, and it cannot be built against a machine-local JSON file — it needs exactly this read path. This issue is its prerequisite.

Note the shape of the mistake, because it is the same one twice: `TI-a9cb3a` and `TI-1ad2f4` were both diagnosed as *write*-path gaps, and both fixes were correct as far as they went. Neither asked whether anything consumed what was now being written. A record nothing reads is not much better than a record that does not exist.

issues.description:
Run the full ingestion path end to end on genuinely new material — research, intake, curation, accession, index sync, retrieval — and report what breaks.

## Why this is worth a dedicated epic

Nearly everything Phase 0 and Phase 1 built is still unexercised on fresh material:

- **Raw source archival** never ran on a real new source. The backfill found zero missing archives because every accepted reference already had one under PDF-only gating, so the HTML path — the entire point of that epic — has never executed against a live fetch.
- **The lexical index** was built over an existing corpus in one pass. Incremental behaviour as references arrive is untested.
- **Assisted curation triage** has never seen a genuinely new prospect. Its lane assignment was measured against a queue that was already stale.
- **The Threat Intelligence publication has 5 accepted references.** Every retrieval measurement in this initiative was taken against a different publication's corpus.

Separately, corpus size — not retrieval quality — is plausibly the binding constraint on publication quality now. Retrieval improved from Hit@5 76% to 96% this week. The corpus did not grow.

## What to do

Work through the path once, deliberately, on a small batch. Ten to twenty prospects is plenty; volume is not the point.

1. **Research.** Use the existing research procedure to find candidate sources on a topic within the threat-intelligence corpus's scope. Do not invent a new mechanism.
2. **Intake.** Confirm prospects land as `pending` references with ingestion rationale preserved, and that nothing becomes evidence without a human.
3. **Triage.** Run `references triage-plan` over the new prospects. Report the lane distribution and — more useful — whether the rationales are specific enough to decide from without opening the source. That question is still open from `kanbus-ec5555`.
4. **Curate.** Accept a handful for real. This is a human decision; surface the queue and stop for the operator rather than deciding.
5. **Accession.** Confirm accepted references get extracted text **and** a `role="source"` archive. **Watch this closely on HTML sources** — this is the archival epic's first live exercise. Verify the S3 object exists, its sha256 matches, and `mediaType` reflects the real content type rather than defaulting to `application/pdf`.
6. **Sync.** Run the vector and lexical index syncs incrementally. Report the audit drift before and after, and whether new references appear in both indexes.
7. **Query.** Ask the knowledge base something only the new references can answer. Confirm they surface, and that a query for an identifier appearing in them hits via the lexical arm.

## What to report

Not "it worked." At each step, what you expected, what you observed, and where they differed. Failures here are the deliverable — every step is a code path that has never run in this configuration.

Specifically worth capturing:
- Anything that required manual intervention that should have been automatic.
- Anything that succeeded but silently did less than expected (the recurring failure mode in this initiative).
- Wall-clock and cost per reference through the full path, which is the real input to any decision about scaling ingestion.

## Constraints

- Use `AWS_PROFILE=papyrus-agent`, never root. See `AGENTS.local.md`.
- **Never create records in a live environment as test fixtures.** Real research on real sources, or stop and ask.
- Curation decisions are the operator's. Prepare the queue; do not accept on their behalf.
- Do not touch `src/papyrus_knowledge_query/` — retrieval work is serial and in flight elsewhere.
- Commit freely, push only when asked.

## Definition of done

A written account of the full path with observations at each step, any defects filed as their own issues, and a small number of genuinely new accepted references in the Threat Intelligence corpus that retrieval can find.

issues.description:
Recency currently measures **when we fetched a document**, not **when it was published**. That inverts the feature's purpose, and it gets worse with every reference we ingest.

## Observed

`ranking.py:126-142` collects day candidates from six keys — `sourceUpdatedAtDay`, `sourcePublishedAtDay`, `retrievedAtDay`, and then the ISO forms `sourceUpdatedAt`, `sourcePublishedAt`, `retrievedAt`, `importedAt` — from both the record and its metadata, then takes `max(day_candidates)`.

`importedAt` and `retrievedAt` are always today-ish for anything we just ingested. So the max is essentially always the ingestion date.

Confirmed live during the recency investigation: the arXiv reference carries `sourcePublishedAtDay=20227` (2025-05-19) and still scores **1.0**, because its retrieve day wins the max.

## Why this matters more than it looks

A recency signal exists so a stale threat-intel report ranks below a fresh one covering the same ground. As written, a 2019 advisory ingested this morning is maximally fresh. The signal reports our crawl schedule.

The failure mode compounds with volume, which is exactly what we are about to do. 43 prospects are queued now and more batches are coming; every one of them will be stamped fresh regardless of source age. If we ever bulk-ingest an archive, the whole archive scores 1.0 and recency becomes actively misleading rather than merely useless.

**This is partly my specification error.** The epic brief said "use `max(sourceUpdatedAtDay, sourcePublishedAtDay)` as the effective date" — I meant max across *publication* dates. Folding in retrieval and import timestamps as additional max candidates is a reasonable reading of "fall back to something", but the result is wrong.

## What it should do

Prefer source dates; never let an operational timestamp beat one.

1. If `sourceUpdatedAt` or `sourcePublishedAt` exists, use `max()` of those two. That was the intent.
2. If neither exists, **do not substitute `retrievedAt` or `importedAt`.** "We don't know when this was published" must not mean "this is brand new." Return neutral (`recencyScore` 0.5, `recencyKnown` false), which is the convention already used for missing quality.
3. Keep the epoch-day fields in metadata regardless — `retrievedAtDay` is useful provenance and may be worth surfacing separately. It just must not drive decay.

Add a test asserting that a record with an old `sourcePublishedAtDay` and a today `retrievedAtDay` scores **old**, not fresh. That is the case that is broken now and the one that will regress silently.

## Related

This also changes the corpus-wide re-sync calculus recorded in the investigation. Stamping `retrievedAtDay` from `importedAt` across 1376 references would have made the entire Papyrus-main corpus uniformly "fresh" while washing out the 316 real publication dates. The recommendation to defer that sync was right; with the current date policy it would have been actively harmful, not merely expensive.

issues.description:
Get the Papyrus knowledge base to a state where the corpus can grow confidently, retrieval works on this domain, and the system surfaces things its operators did not think to ask for — without breaking the cost model or the editorial guarantees.

**Full design doc**: `docs/knowledge-retrieval-roadmap.md`. Architecture orientation: `project/wiki/knowledge-base-architecture.md`. Current retrieval path: `docs/internal-knowledge-research.md`.

## The goal

Papyrus is meant to be **steered, not operated**. That implies a knowledge base that covers ground the operator did not individually specify, sources everything it claims, and does not require a human to shepherd each document through by hand. We are not there. Getting there needs four things that are currently missing or weak: sources we cannot lose, a way to tell whether a change helped, retrieval that handles this domain's exact identifiers and freshness, and a discovery mechanism that is not purely reactive.

## What is actually constraining us

Three constraints, in the order they bite.

**1. Curation throughput.** Every accepted reference passes through one human. The corpus is small because of that gate. It is also the gate that makes citations trustworthy and keeps per-document LLM spend bounded, so it stays — but almost everything else in this initiative improves machinery *downstream* of it. Assisted triage (automating around the decision without automating the decision) is therefore the highest-leverage single epic here, and it is easy to overlook precisely because it is not a retrieval problem.

**2. Source durability.** Ingestion has been deliberately throttled out of a concern that a large import would need re-importing after an architecture change. Being precise about that concern is clarifying:

- *Safely re-derivable from what we already store*: chunking, embedding model, distillation artifacts, entity extraction, entity resolution, contextual prefixes, the entire vector index. All regenerate from `extracted_text` attachments plus the GraphQL records. No re-import, ever.
- *NOT re-derivable*: anything needing the original fetched artifact. Raw bytes are archived only for PDFs today (`_reference_source_attachment_record` is gated on `_looks_like_pdf_uri` / `is_pdf_source` at `reference_url_text.py:166` and `:257`), so accepted HTML references keep extracted text and nothing else. Threat-intel sources get revised, pulled, and paywalled.

That single gap — not the retrieval architecture — is what genuinely gates safe corpus growth.

**3. Retrieval quality.** Retrieval is embedding-only (OpenAI text-embedding-3-small → S3 Vectors, 1536-dim cosine). For a threat-intelligence publication this is the worst available single-retriever weakness: CVE IDs, hashes, actor aliases, domains, and ATT&CK IDs are exact-token queries that embeddings blur. There is no recency signal (dates are not even in vector metadata), no rank fusion, and no rerank — plus two latent defects: passage scoring carries hardcoded boosts tuned for a prior AI/ML-research corpus, and an 8-chunk cap means only the first ~1,440 words of long reports are searchable. And none of it is measurable today.

## Where the ideas came from

Two external sources informed the technical approach. They are inputs, not the organizing principle.

1. Cerebras Engineering, "How We Built Our Knowledge Base" (Tai, Kim, Gao, July 2026) — https://www.cerebras.ai/blog/how-we-built-our-knowledge-base. Production system, 15,000+ queries/day. **Retrieval-centric**: how do I find the right thing? Core lesson — never trust a single retrieval technique; run several and fuse the ranked lists.
2. "Graph Engineering: 4 Models to 4 Prompts" (Boris Cherny, Full Course From Scratch, July 2026) — independently compiled from Anthropic's Knowledge Graph Cookbook and related docs; **not an Anthropic publication and not endorsed by Anthropic**, demonstration corpus is six Wikipedia articles, so treat its techniques as sound and its numbers as illustrative. **Representation-centric**: how do I represent what a document says? Its most transferable idea is that a grounded one-line entity description written during extraction is what makes later resolution possible.

They compose rather than compete. Note that graph traversal has a cold-start problem the second source does not address — traversal needs a seed entity, and search is how you find one.

What Papyrus already does as well or better than either: curation gating, knowledge-graph expansion, quality-aware ranking, token-budgeted context packs, versioned lineage. We already have the graph the second source describes building; what we lack is a pipeline that populates it densely.

## Status — corrected 2026-07-27

Two claims previously recorded here were wrong. Both are corrected below rather than deleted, because the way they came to be wrong is the lesson.

**Landed and holding:**
- *Raw source archival* (P0, `88ab2a`) — link-rot insurance. Backfill found the exposure was **prospective, not historical**: every accepted reference already had an archive under PDF-only gating. This protects future HTML ingestion.
- *Retrieval eval harness* (P0, `8e3252`) — 25 golden queries, baseline MRR 0.653 / Hit@5 76%, provenance-labelled. Noise floor measured: ranks 1-5 reliable, 6-8 are noise. **Covers `ai-ml-research` only.**
- *Delete dead ranking config* (P1, `ca0de0`) — net −232 lines, proven behaviour-neutral. `reporting` consumer profile kept: `reporter.tac` uses it, contrary to the brief.
- *Passage-scoring cleanup* (P1, `5c7cde`) — recorded as **unverified**: the golden set scores which reference ranks, not which passage is selected.

**Correction 1 — hybrid lexical is not currently working.** `a61c12` is closed and this section previously read "identifier 0/5 → 5/5 … the central premise is now confirmed empirically." As of 2026-07-27 the identifier category scores **0/5 on `develop`** and global MRR is **0.6533 — exactly the pre-hybrid baseline**, i.e. the lexical arm is contributing nothing at all. Filed as **`TI-b9f6da` (P0)**. The premise may well be sound; it is not currently demonstrated, and nothing measured downstream of a broken retriever can be trusted until it is.

The long-carried footnote — "pending explanation of a 99-reference gap between the lexical artifact (1321) and the live accepted corpus (1420)" — was a warning that went unread for weeks. It is now a required, measured field in every eval report.

**Correction 2 — age decay is installed but unfed.** `bb12d3` is closed as delivered. Publication-date coverage is **316/1376 (23.0%)** on ai-ml-research and **1/13 (7.7%)** on threat-intelligence, so recency is a near-constant for most of the corpus and moves nothing. The post-hybrid and post-recency reports are identical to four decimals, `mrr_sum` included — landing the epic changed nothing measurable. Filed as **`TI-06361a` (P1)**. `TI-f1cc13` correctly stopped ingestion timestamps from masquerading as publication dates; it made the signal honest, not live.

**Done, pending merge:**
- `TI-f1cc13` — recency prefers publication dates. Branch `fix/recency-prefer-publication-date`, commits `bfc2f33` + `5571596`. Reviewed and correct.
- `TI-c21d28` — curation triage state in GraphQL. Branch `epic/c21d28-triage-graphql`, commit `37932c2`. Reviewed and correct. **Blocked on a sandbox schema deploy**, which needs a CloudFormation-capable profile; `papyrus-agent` is denied that by design. Human step.

## Sequencing — revised

AD-4 still governs: retrieval-changing epics land serially.

**Order:**
1. **`TI-b9f6da` (P0)** — restore the lexical arm. Everything else measured against the golden set is meaningless until this is fixed. Nothing else in retrieval should start first.
2. **`TI-5ed2f2` (raised P2 → P1)** — repeatable eval environments. This regression sat undetected across at least two landings and was found only by accident, while an agent was verifying something else. The harness cannot currently distinguish "my change broke it" from "the environment drifted," which is most of what an eval is for.
3. **`TI-06361a` (P1)** — publication-date extraction, so recency has something to act on.
4. **`TI-70c76b` (P1, decision)** — the threat-intelligence corpus is **13 references** and TI identifier retrieval has never been measured. Read before starting Phase 2.

**Phase 2 (entity extraction → resolution → contextual chunks) is on hold pending `TI-70c76b`.** Its own sequencing note says resolution "deliberately follows corpus growth: resolution's value is proportional to alias fragmentation, which barely exists yet." At 13 documents there is nothing to resolve. The precondition has not been met.

**Parallel-safe** (different subsystems): assisted curation triage follow-ons, the 3 blocked references, heading weights to per-corpus config.

## The pattern worth naming

Every significant defect in this initiative has been the same shape: **silent partial work that looks like success.** `except: pass` disabling archival. An index publishing itself smaller. Records written that nothing reads. An eval measuring the wrong dimension. And now a retrieval arm contributing nothing while the suite still reports a number.

Each was caught late and by accident. The countermeasure is not more review — it is that every component which can silently do nothing must be made to say so at the point it happens, and every eval must record the size of what it measured. Prefer a loud failure to a plausible number.

## Architectural decisions (current)

### AD-1: Graph traversal is a RETRIEVER, not a separate answering mode

When graph-grounded retrieval matures it contributes a ranked list fused (RRF) alongside semantic and lexical lists — not a second query pipeline with its own LLM call.

Why: the engine ALREADY blends graph signal into one ranked list via hand-tuned constants in `_rank_structured_records` (`engine.py:2161-2180`). Fusion is continuous with existing architecture; RRF replaces those arbitrary constants with a principled rank-consensus score, deleting heuristics rather than adding machinery. A separate mode would require a query-time LLM call, breaking the LLM-free-at-query-time property we protect everywhere except the feature-flagged reranker, plus query entity-linking to find seeds — whereas under fusion the seeds come free from semantic/lexical hits.

**Consequence**: `fuse_ranked_lists()` MUST accept N ranked lists with per-list weights from day one.

### AD-2: Entity metadata augments retrieval; it never gates it (v1)

Entity metadata boosts and joins; it is not a restrictive filter until extraction recall is measured. Incomplete metadata used as an exclusion filter silently hides material with total confidence. The dangerous failure of extraction is omission, not hallucination.

### AD-3: Entity merges need a curation gate

Resolution errors are EDITORIAL errors. Merging two distinct threat actors makes the publication issue false attribution claims laundered through its own citation machinery. Merges land as proposals requiring human confirmation; un-merging stays cheap.

### AD-4: Retrieval-changing epics land serially, not in parallel

Phase B's four epics touch the same files within lines of each other. Concurrent dispatch produces merge conflicts at best and semantic conflicts at worst.

## Hard constraints (non-negotiable)

1. **Scale to zero.** No provisioned-capacity services, no always-on components, no fixed monthly floors. This is why OpenSearch is disqualified (~$350/month floor × N instances).
2. **Fleet of single-publication instances, NOT multi-tenant.** Each installation is one publication with its own stack. Never introduce tenant awareness.
3. **The knowledge-query Lambda is stdlib-only.** It bundles by copying `src/papyrus_knowledge_query` verbatim with an intentionally empty requirements.txt. Python 3.12, ARM64, 512 MB.
4. **The curation gate stays.** Automate around the human decision, never the decision itself. No confidence score may become an auto-accept threshold.

## For implementers

- **This plan is not frozen.** It records current decisions and their reasoning so nobody re-derives them from scratch. Model capability moves quickly and we intend to re-examine this as it does — challenge any decision here if you have information we did not.
- Verify every file:line reference before editing — they were verified 2026-07-25 and drift as epics merge.
- Tests live in `procedures/newsroom/tests/` (see `test_knowledge_query.py`). Add tests with every change.
- Local smoke: `PYTHONPATH=src python -m papyrus_newsroom knowledge-query --query "..." --format structured --execution local`.
- Report before/after golden-set numbers on any retrieval-changing PR — as a regression tripwire, not a score to maximize.
- Work through the Kanbus CLI; do not edit `project/` JSON directly (`CONTRIBUTING_AGENT.template.md`). Wiki markdown under `project/wiki/` may be edited directly.
- Repo-visible content constraint: keep examples generic (CVE IDs, hashes, domains).

comments.text:
## Design decision — v1 assisted triage (CLI-first)

Given empty rejection history, v1 will **not** pretend to learn likely-reject from labels we do not have. Shipping a valuable operator loop now:

### Commands
- `papyrus references triage-plan --corpus-key threat-intelligence` — build a run under `.papyrus-runs/assisted-triage-<id>/` with lanes, clusters, grounded rationales, and mechanical auto-reject candidates. Dry-run by default for mutations.
- `papyrus references triage-review --plan <manifest>` — keyboard-driven one-decision-per-screen session (`a` accept / `r` reject+reason / `s` skip / `q` quit). **Accept only on explicit keypress.** Metrics written to session log.
- `papyrus references triage-auto-reject --plan <manifest>` — apply only mechanical auto-rejects from the plan (logged, enumerable).
- `papyrus references triage-auto-rejects` / `triage-reverse-auto-reject` — list and reverse auto-rejects via reopen.

### Lane assignment (history-aware, thin-data safe)
- **likely-accept**: concrete overlap with an accepted reference (shared domain + title tokens, or high title Jaccard to a named accepted ref).
- **likely-reject**: similarity to rejected refs with `out_of_scope`/`policy_exclusion` when that history exists; or non-primary members of a cluster whose primary is already accepted (still human-gated unless exact mechanical duplicate).
- **uncertain**: default when signal is thin — expected to be the largest lane today.
- **exploratory** metadata (`metadata.exploratory` / provenance) → labeled and **exempt** from history-based scoring (always uncertain for review).

### Mechanical auto-reject only
- exact `sourceUri` (normalized) already accepted
- exact URI previously rejected
- citation stub with no URI, no DOI, no source/extracted_text attachment (unavailable)
- Never auto-accept. Never editorial auto-reject.

### Rationales
Template-grounded, checkable facts only (named accepted/rejected ref titles/ids, cluster siblings, missing URI/attachments). No generic “seems relevant” prose.

### Deferred (child stories if needed)
- Newsroom UI batch review surface
- Live HTTP dead-link probing at plan time (optional; stubs-without-material cover the bulk of today’s mechanical unusable set)
- Calibrated ML lane model once rejection reason-codes accumulate

### What shipped
CLI-first assisted triage that automates everything *around* the curation decision and never the decision itself.

**New commands**
```bash
# Build lanes, clusters, grounded rationales, mechanical auto-reject candidates
PYTHONPATH=src python -m papyrus.cli references triage-plan \
  --corpus-key threat-intelligence

# Keyboard review session (default dry-run). Keys: a/r/s/q
PYTHONPATH=src python -m papyrus.cli references triage-review \
  --plan .papyrus-runs/assisted-triage-<id>/plan.json \
  --lanes uncertain
# Write decisions only with:
#   --apply-decisions

PYTHONPATH=src python -m papyrus.cli references triage-auto-reject \
  --plan .papyrus-runs/assisted-triage-<id>/plan.json
# Write with: --apply-auto-rejects

PYTHONPATH=src python -m papyrus.cli references triage-auto-rejects \
  --corpus-key threat-intelligence
PYTHONPATH=src python -m papyrus.cli references triage-reverse-auto-reject \
  --reference <id> --dry-run false
```

**Core module:** `src/papyrus_content/assisted_curation_triage.py`  
**CLI wiring:** `references_commands.py`, `cli.py`  
**Audit hook:** `review_reference_curation(..., auto_reject_rule=)` persists `autoReject` / `autoRejectRule` / `reversible` on curation Messages. Accept + auto_reject_rule is refused.

- `autoAcceptDisabled: true` on every plan
- Acceptance only via explicit human `a` in `triage-review` (or existing `review-curation`)
- Auto-reject rules are mechanical only: `duplicate_of_accepted_uri`, `prior_rejected_uri`, `mechanically_unavailable`

| Signal | Result |
|---|---|
| pending | 1793 |
| accepted | 5 |
| rejected / reason-codes | **0 / empty** |
| title near-dup groups | 92 (200 members) |
| URI-less citation stubs | ~815 |

- human queue: 135 (after dedupe + auto-reject filtering)
- auto-reject candidates: **265** mechanically unavailable stubs
- clusters: 11
- lanes: uncertain 135 / likely-accept 0 / likely-reject 0 (thin history)

comments.text:
Went through this properly rather than just reading your summary — it's good work. Reopening the issue, but not because anything's broken; the acceptance criterion is behavioural and we haven't actually exercised it yet. Stuff to do at the bottom.

First though: thank you for measuring before designing, and for saying plainly that the result contradicted the brief. I wrote that line about accept/reject history being "the most under-exploited asset in the codebase" and it was just wrong — 5 accepted, 0 rejected, no reason codes anywhere. You could easily have built the history-based scoring anyway and it would have looked fine and done nothing. Instead you reported the gap, adjusted to similarity plus mechanical signals, and left the history path wired so it strengthens as rejections accumulate. That's the right call and I'd rather be corrected than agreed with.

The safety side is genuinely well done. It's enforced in code rather than described in comments: the accept path raises if it ever sees an auto-rule, the review session refuses to start unless the plan carries `acceptanceRequiresExplicitHumanAction`, and auto-rejects are tagged and reversible with a command to undo them. All three auto-reject rules are mechanical, nothing editorial snuck in. That was the hardest requirement in the epic and you got it right.

Your two findings are worth more than the code, honestly — 815 pending stubs with no sourceUri or DOI, and 92 title-duplicate groups covering 200 members. Neither was on anyone's radar.

One thing worth sitting with before the next step. With 5 accepted and 0 rejected, lane assignment has almost nothing to work with, so most of the 1793 will land in `uncertain`. issues.description:
Automate everything around the curation decision without automating the decision itself, so human attention goes to the cases that actually need judgment.

## Why this is the highest-leverage epic on the board

Curation throughput is the binding constraint on this publication's knowledge. Every accepted reference passes through one human. The corpus is small *because* of that gate, not despite it — and almost every other epic in this initiative improves the machinery **downstream** of the constraint. Optimizing a non-bottleneck produces no throughput.

The gate itself must stay. It is what makes a citation in a published article traceable to a source someone chose, and it is the cost governor that keeps per-document LLM spend bounded. The goal is not to remove it but to stop spending human attention on the parts of it that are not judgment.

## The distinction this epic rests on

Two different things travel under the word "curation":

**Judgment** — is this source credible, relevant, and worth this publication's attention? Irreducibly human. Do not automate. Do not add a "confidence" score that quietly becomes an auto-accept threshold.

**Everything surrounding judgment** — deduplication, triage, ordering, pre-summarization, filtering the obviously unusable, and articulating *why* a prospect might matter. All machine work, all currently costing the operator attention that judgment needs.

## Design directions

1. **Pre-sort the queue into three lanes**: likely-accept, likely-reject, and genuinely-uncertain. The operator works the uncertain lane carefully and skims the other two. The uncertain lane is the product; the other two are conveniences.
2. **Lead every prospect with a rationale, not metadata.** One or two sentences on why this might matter *to this publication* — what it connects to in the existing corpus, what coverage gap it fills, who else we have accepted that cites it. A URL and a title force the operator to reconstruct context that the machine already has.
3. **The training signal already exists.** Rejected references are retained as scope memory rather than deleted, so the system has been quietly accumulating labeled examples of what this publication decided *not* to cover. Use accepted-vs-rejected history as the basis for lane assignment. This is the most under-exploited asset in the codebase.
4. **Deduplicate hard before the human sees anything.** Same story from five vendors is one decision, not five. Cluster near-duplicate prospects and present the cluster with the best-sourced member surfaced.
5. **Batch review ergonomics.** The gate fails not by being absent but by being tedious — thirty prompts of which twenty-nine are obvious produces rubber-stamping, and a rubber-stamped gate is worse than an honest absence because it still confers the appearance of review. Design for the bored reviewer: keyboard-driven, one screen per decision, no context-switching to look things up.
6. **Auto-reject is allowed only for the mechanically unusable** — dead links, paywalls with no extractable text, duplicates of already-accepted sources, sources already rejected under a prior URL. Anything requiring an editorial opinion goes to a human. Log every auto-reject so the rule set stays auditable and reversible.
7. **Measure throughput honestly**: prospects reviewed per session, time-to-decision, and the accept rate *within each lane*. If the likely-accept lane is frequently rejected the lane assignment is miscalibrated, and skimming it becomes dangerous.

## Relationship to other epics

- **Blocks nothing formally, but should land before or alongside the exploratory-research epic.** Exploration adds review volume; adding volume to a saturated bottleneck makes the situation worse, not better.
- **Benefits from entity extraction** — extracted entities make "what does this connect to" answerable — but must not wait for it; a v1 based on corpus similarity and rejection history is valuable on its own.
- **Independent of all retrieval work.** Different files, different concerns. Can proceed in parallel with anything.

## What could go wrong

- **Lane assignment becomes an auto-accept threshold.** The most likely failure and the most damaging: the moment likely-accept is trusted enough to skip, the curation gate is gone and nobody notices, because the artifact of review still exists. Keep acceptance an explicit human action, always.
- **Rationales that are plausible but wrong** train the operator to distrust them, after which the feature is dead weight. Ground every rationale in something concrete and checkable — a specific existing reference, a named coverage gap — not in generic assessment.
- **Optimizing for queue-empty rather than decision quality.** Faster rejection is not the goal; the goal is more attention available for the cases that reward it.
- **Rejection history encodes past blind spots.** Training lane assignment on prior decisions will faithfully reproduce whatever the operator has been systematically overlooking. This is in direct tension with the exploratory-research epic, and it is why exploratory prospects should be labeled as such and exempted from history-based lane assignment.

## Acceptance criteria

- A review session over a realistic prospect batch demonstrably takes less operator time per decision than today, with no reduction in decision quality on a hand-checked sample.
- No path exists by which a reference becomes accepted without an explicit human action.
- Auto-rejects are logged, enumerable, and reversible.

Add named scope bundles so a query can say `scopeName: "apt-desk"` instead of hand-assembling corpus/category/kind filters, and so desks and procedures get sensible defaults. Cerebras calls these "projects"; ours operate entirely within one publication instance (desks, corpora, initiatives) — the publication boundary is the installation itself, so bundles never need publication awareness.

## Current state (verified 2026-07-19)

- The filter mechanism exists end-to-end: scope keys pass through `_normalize_request` (`src/papyrus_knowledge_query/engine.py:298-419`) to the S3 Vectors metadata filter (`_metadata_filter`, `services.py:397-433`; supports corpusId, categorySetId, classifierId, curationStatus, vectorKind and more).
- Tactus procedures already inject per-procedure scope defaults: `knowledge_query_scope` parameter (`src/papyrus_newsroom/tactus_runtime.py:1112`) parsed and merged in Lua (`parse_requested_knowledge_scope`, `tactus_runtime.py:1251-1290`) — this demonstrates the intended merge pattern (defaults under explicit values).
- The knowledge-query CLI (`src/papyrus_knowledge_query/cli.py:203-226`) builds scope from kind flags only — no corpus flag, no bundle concept.
- Unknown-value handling convention to copy: unknown ranking profile → warning + fallback (`ranking.py:53-59`).

## Design decisions (current thinking — challenge them if you have better information)

1. **Registry = a JSON file inside the package: `src/papyrus_knowledge_query/scope_bundles.json`.** JSON, not YAML — the Lambda is stdlib-only and pyyaml is not available. The file ships to the Lambda automatically because bundling copies the package verbatim. A freshly spun-up instance ships a starter file; per-instance customization is a repo edit + deploy (acceptable at this stage; an S3-override env var is a noted follow-up, not v1).
2. **Schema**: `{"bundles": {"<name>": {"description": str, "scope": {<any keys _normalize_request accepts>}, "ranking": {"profile": str, "diversity": str}}}}`. Validate bundle scope keys against the known-key set at load; warn on unknown keys rather than failing.
3. **Resolution**: new `scope.scopeName` handled early in `_normalize_request`: load bundle, apply its scope/ranking values as DEFAULTS, then let explicitly provided request keys override. Unknown scopeName → append warning, proceed unscoped (mirror the ranking-profile convention). Lazy-load + cache the registry at module level.
4. **CLI**: add `--scope-name` to the knowledge-query command; list available bundles in `--help` epilog or a `--list-scopes` flag (implementer's choice, document it).
5. **Tactus**: allow `knowledge_query_scope` defaults to carry `scopeName` so a procedure (e.g. reporter) can pin a desk bundle; the existing Lua merge already passes unknown scope keys through — verify, don't assume.
6. **Starter bundles for this instance**: `"default"` (empty scope — documents the schema), `"accepted-references"` (curationStatus accepted, reference kinds). Do NOT invent desk-specific bundles without checking actual corpusId values in the deployed data — leave a TODO listing where to find them (`KnowledgeCorpus` records via GraphQL).

## Files to modify

- NEW `src/papyrus_knowledge_query/scope_bundles.json` — starter registry.
- NEW loader (either in `engine.py` or a small `scope_bundles.py` module — prefer the module; keep engine.py from growing).
- `src/papyrus_knowledge_query/engine.py` — `_normalize_request` resolution.
- `src/papyrus_knowledge_query/cli.py` — `--scope-name`.
- `src/papyrus_newsroom/tactus_runtime.py` — only if scopeName doesn't already pass through the Lua scope merge (verify first).
- `procedures/newsroom/tests/test_knowledge_query.py` — merge-precedence tests (bundle default vs explicit override), unknown-name warning test, unknown-key-in-bundle warning test.

## What could go wrong

- **Precedence bugs are the whole risk.** The invariant: explicit request keys ALWAYS beat bundle values; bundle values ALWAYS beat engine defaults. Test all three layers in one test.
- **Key drift**: `_normalize_request` accepts a specific key set that will grow (dates, entity filters from other epics). The bundle validator must warn-not-fail on unknown keys so an old deploy doesn't break on a newer bundle file.
- **The Lambda reads the packaged file** — use a path relative to `__file__` (or importlib.resources), never CWD, or it breaks in the Lambda bundle layout.
- **Ranking overrides**: bundle ranking.profile must flow through `normalize_ranking_config` (which validates), not bypass it.

## Out of scope

S3-hosted runtime-editable registry (follow-up), per-user defaults (not a newsroom concept), any UI.

Own the vector-index rebuilds that several epics depend on. This exists as its own tracked task because "batch the rebuilds" is an instruction to PEOPLE, written across three epic briefs that different agents will finish weeks apart. The predictable failure: features merge, nobody runs the rebuild, retrieval behavior does not change, and everyone assumes the work is done.

A feature that requires a rebuild is NOT done when its PR merges. It is done when the rebuild has run and the eval harness confirms the effect.

## Trigger conditions

**Rebuild A — metadata only (cheap, no re-embed).**
Trigger: the age-decay epic has merged.
Effect: writes `sourcePublishedAtDay` / `sourceUpdatedAtDay` / `retrievedAtDay` into vector metadata. Until it runs, age decay is a silent no-op for vector matches (missing dates score neutral) — backward-compatible, so it may ride along with any convenient sync rather than forcing its own run.

**Rebuild B — full re-embed (the expensive one).**
Trigger: BOTH the entity-extraction epic AND the contextual-chunks epic have merged.
Effect: changes embedding INPUT (distilled artifact text; contextual chunk prefixes) and lifts the per-reference chunk cap. Do NOT run this after only one of the two lands — that is two re-embeds where one would do.
Cost at current corpus size: dollars, not hundreds. Verify with a dry run first.

## Procedure

1. Run the eval harness and record the pre-rebuild baseline.
2. Dry-run the index operation first (`--dry-run` / `--action audit`) and read the reported deltas: reference count, chunk count, gated-chunk count, artifact sizes. Sanity-check that the vector-count delta is explainable before writing anything.
3. Run the rebuild (`knowledge vector-index --action rebuild`, or `sync --force` where sufficient — confirm which against `src/papyrus_knowledge_query/vector_index.py` `index_reference_passages` semantics at the time).
4. Re-run the eval harness. Compare per-category, not just aggregate.
5. Record both reports and the observed cost in a comment on this task.
6. If results regress, the rebuild is not "done" — open a follow-up rather than leaving the corpus in a worse state.

## What could go wrong

- **Nobody runs it.** The whole reason this task exists. Whoever merges the triggering epic must move this task to in_progress.
- **Half-batched Rebuild B** — running after extraction lands but before contextual chunks (or vice versa) doubles the cost for no benefit. Check both epics are merged.
- **Positional chunk keys**: chunk vector keys are `sha256(lineageId:storagePath:chunkIndex)`, so changing embedded TEXT does not change the key. A plain `sync` may consider existing chunks already present and skip them. Confirm whether `rebuild` or `--force` is required for embeddings to actually refresh — this is the single most likely way to "run the rebuild" and have nothing change.
- **Partial-failure states**: a rebuild that dies midway can leave the index mixed-generation. Confirm the operation's resumability and, if it is not resumable, run it in a window where it can complete.
